newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-Mountbatten's India plan passes muster.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Mountbatten's India plan passes muster.

text.p: At a two-hour conference with Indian leaders in his study at the Viceroy's House, Lord Louis Mountbatten handed round copies of The Partition Plan.

Mountbatten, the last viceroy of India before it won freedom from British colonial rule in August 1947, was passing around the blueprint for what was to be the blood-stained partition of the subcontinent into India and Pakistan.
The leaders included Jawaharlal Nehru, who would be independent India's first prime minister, Mohammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan, and five others.

The viceroy made it clear he was not forcing the pace but everybody he had spoken to wanted an end to the present state of uncertainty, communal tension and friction. So the sooner power was transferred, the better for all.
Mountbatten was in masterly form. His opening remarks were a challenge to them to rise to the level of events they were creating.
TRANSFER OF POWER SOONER THAN EXPECTED

Worth noting here is that just months previously, London pundits were questioning whether independence in the second half of 1948 was not too rushed. Even up to April 1947, Mountbatten had been telling governors that June 1948 was a firm departure date. Now, August 15, 1947, was being hinted at.
Mountbatten was sometimes charged with being too hasty. "I would like to have more time but time was not on our side", he said years later.
He quoted an Indian leader as saying: "If you had not transferred power when you did, there would have been no power to transfer."

Mountbatten had earlier told the leaders he felt he would be asking them to go against their consciences if he sought full agreement. He was merely asking them to accept the plan in a peaceful spirit for the good of the country.

Nehru said there could never be complete approval of the plan by Indian National Congress but on balance they accepted it. Congress, still a powerful party in modern Indian politics, was formed in 1885 and spearheaded the independence movement.
Jinnah considered the viceroy had correctly interpreted and recorded his views.
THE PARTITION PLAN
From that moment, Mountbatten knew the essential battle was won.

And it was the signal for him to throw on the table copies of a lengthy paper -- "The Administrative Consequences of Partition" -- 34 pages of foolscap prepared by the viceroy's staff bringing the leaders right up against the hard executive realities of their political decision.
"The severe shock this gave to everyone present would have been amusing if it was not rather tragic," said Mountbatten afterwards.
Mountbatten got Nehru and Jinnah to agree to follow him with broadcasts to the people of India the following night.
Mountbatten's broadcast was subdued and balanced.
Nehru was moving, as he could be so eloquent on big occasions -- "We are little men serving great causes, and because the cause is great, something of that greatness falls upon us also."

Jinnah's followers thought his broadcast a masterpiece -- "It is for us to consider whether the plan as presented to us by His Majesty's government should be accepted by us as a compromise or a settlement. On this point I do not wish to prejudge," he said.
The next day, Mountbatten unveiled the plan for the partition of India to 300 Indian and foreign newsmen.
It was a scintillating performance -- a 45-minute exposition without notes of a political plan of daunting complexity followed by about 100 questions, most of them from Indian correspondents.
Only twice did Mountbatten refer to a member of his staff. He showed brilliance, dexterity and a light-hearted touch that won applause.

When a correspondent tried to draw him on Jinnah's recent demand for a land corridor through India linking East and West Pakistan -- a point never discussed in the plan -- he replied in a flash: "Which paragraph in the plan are you referring to?"
He also gave the first public informal indication that August 15, 1947, would be the likely date for the transfer of power to the two new nations.
THE GANDHI PLAN

Mountbatten invited Mahatma Gandhi, the spiritual father of independent India, to call round that evening and urged him to consider the announcement not as a Mountbatten Plan but as a Gandhi Plan, incorporating all Gandhi's major concepts of non-coercion, self-determination and the earliest possible date of British departure.

Partition was undoubtedly a tragedy but a worse tragedy would have been to try to impose a unity unacceptable to the great majority of 100 million Moslems -- that was a widely held detached view of the implications of Partition at that time.
Mountbatten succeeded. At his prayer meeting that June night, Gandhi said: "The British government is not responsible for partition. The viceroy had no hand in it.
"In fact he is as opposed to division as Congress itself, but if both of us -- Hindus and Moslems -- can not agree to anything else, then the viceroy is left with no choice."
